problemSolved: Models jump straight to a default aesthetic instead of reasoning about who the site is for and what it should feel like.
mechanism: Before any code, the model must read five concrete signal types (page kind, vibe words, reference links, audience, quiet constraints) and emit one committed sentence: 'Reading this as: <page kind> for <audience>, with a <vibe> language, leaning toward <system/aesthetic family>.' Only if the read genuinely diverges does it ask ONE clarifying question; otherwise it commits and proceeds.
whyItWorks: It forces the model to externalize a judgment call as text before generation starts, which is exactly the 'reasoning natively from evidence' behavior the C-no-mechanical-creativity brief measured at 59 vs. 40 for template generation. Committing to one sentence also prevents the model from hedging across multiple aesthetics inside one build.
outputImpact: Directly determines every downstream decision (dials, design-system choice, palette, layout family) — this is the single highest-leverage mechanism in the file.
failureModes: a bad or generic 'design read' silently propagates into a bad build with nothing downstream able to catch it
no mechanism forces the read to be revisited if later sections contradict it
testMethod: asserted only — the checklist (line 916) asks 'declared?' as a yes/no, not a quality bar
sitesmithForm: Keep as the mandatory first move of the unified skill: one committed sentence, evidence-cited, before any file is written. Do not turn it into a form with dropdowns — the value is in forcing prose reasoning, not selection.

problemSolved: Agents either guess wrong silently or dump a multi-question interrogation back at the user before doing any work.
mechanism: Ask exactly one question, only when the design read genuinely diverges; otherwise infer confidently and proceed without asking.
whyItWorks: Bounds the interrogation failure mode without removing the ability to ask when it actually matters — matches the 'ask only when it would materially change scope' instinct SiteSmith already wants.
requiredContext: design read from the prior step
outputImpact: Reduces friction; does not change visual output directly.
failureModes: no criterion is given for what counts as 'genuinely diverges' beyond the model's own judgment — unfalsifiable in practice
sitesmithForm: State the rule plainly: one question max, only when two plausible reads would produce materially different builds.

problemSolved: Gives the model and the user a shared vocabulary to talk about how experimental, animated, and dense a design should be, instead of vague words like 'make it pop.'
mechanism: Three named 1-10 scales (DESIGN_VARIANCE, MOTION_INTENSITY, VISUAL_DENSITY) with a baseline (8/6/4) and two lookup tables that assign numeric ranges from vibe words (§1.A) or use-case presets (§1.B), e.g. 'minimalist/clean/calm' → variance 5-6.
whyItWorks: As shared vocabulary it is genuinely useful for communicating intent concisely. As a *decision mechanism* it is a table lookup, not reasoning — exactly the pattern the brief's C-no-mechanical-creativity axis flags as a liability when it substitutes for judgment rather than summarizing it.
outputImpact: Gates almost every downstream section (layout asymmetry, animation choreography, section padding) — high leverage but also high convergence risk since the baseline 8/6/4 is the default absent an override.
failureModes: stateless lookup tables produce the same three numbers for the same vibe words across unrelated projects, which is a structural driver of the exact convergence problem in C-no-house-style
numeric dials give a false sense of precision/objectivity for what is actually a qualitative judgment
conflicts: C-no-house-style: deterministic vibe-word→number tables are a rules engine, not a design read
testMethod: none — the checklist only asks 'dial values explicit and reasoned, not silently using baseline?' (line 917), which cannot verify reasoning quality
sitesmithForm: Keep the three named concepts as vocabulary the model uses in its own reasoning prose ('this reads as high-variance, restrained-motion, low-density'). Drop the numeric 1-10 scale and the vibe-word→number lookup tables entirely — they are the mechanical-substitution failure mode, not the useful part.

problemSolved: LLMs hand-roll CSS that badly imitates Fluent/Material/Carbon/GOV.UK/etc. instead of using the real, accessible, official package — or conversely treat a pure aesthetic (bento, brutalism, glassmorphism) as if it had one official source.
mechanism: A two-bucket routing table: brief matches a named enterprise/gov design system → install and use the official package verbatim, never recreate its CSS by hand, never mix two systems in one tree (§2.A, with install commands and canonical doc URLs vendored in Appendix A/B). Brief is an aesthetic with no owning package → build with native CSS/Tailwind and say so honestly in comments (§2.B), including an explicit callout that 'Apple Liquid Glass' has no public web CSS package and any implementation is a labeled approximation (Appendix C).
whyItWorks: This is a grounding mechanism, not a creative one — it prevents a specific class of hallucination (inventing a framework, or claiming a home-rolled effect is an official Apple/Google technology) by giving the model a checkable fact table instead of asking it to recall package names from training data.
requiredContext: Appendix B doc links only when the system route is taken
contextCost: medium (the appendix table is ~120 lines, only needed conditionally)
outputImpact: Prevents a specific, recurring, verifiable class of factual error (wrong install command, invented CSS-only 'liquid glass' library) without touching the creative decision at all.
failureModes: package names and APIs go stale (e.g. `@fluentui/web-components` version drift) since this is static vendored text, not a live doc fetch
testMethod: none in-repo, but is trivially checkable against real package registries
sitesmithForm: Port the two-bucket logic and the 'label honestly if it's an approximation' rule as-is; re-verify the install commands and doc links at rebuild time rather than copying them verbatim (see LICENSE.md — these are facts, not the source's creative expression, so re-verification is preferable to reuse anyway).

problemSolved: Blocklisting known LLM-default tells (Inter as default sans, AI-purple, three-equal-cards, em-dash, generic names, filler verbs) without permanently outlawing them for the rare brief that actually wants them.
mechanism: Every ban is written as 'X is discouraged/banned as a DEFAULT' followed by an explicit 'Override:' clause naming the exact condition under which X becomes acceptable again (e.g. Inter is fine for an explicitly neutral/Linear-style or public-sector brief; serif is fine only if the brief literally names one or the aesthetic family is genuinely editorial/luxury/heritage).
whyItWorks: A ban with a stated override condition is falsifiable and revisitable by the model in-context; a bare ban either gets ignored (models 'historically ignored em-dash limits when phrased as sparingly', line 701) or, if made absolute with no exception (the em-dash ban, §9.G), becomes trivially machine-checkable with a single regex scan for `—`/`–`.
requiredContext: design read to evaluate whether an override condition is met
contextCost: high in aggregate — sections 4 and 9 alone are ~540 lines of banned-pattern enumeration
outputImpact: Directly reduces the most commonly cited 'AI slop' tells (verified against the file's own claimed production-test provenance in §9.F, though that provenance is asserted, not published — see TESTING.md).
failureModes: banning specific named cliches (Fraunces, Instrument Serif, exact beige/brass hex codes) only holds until the *next* wave of LLM-default cliches emerges — this is whack-a-mole, not a durable mechanism, and needs periodic re-curation
an absolute ban with no override (em-dash) is the only reliably enforceable member of this family; everything else depends on the model correctly judging whether its own override condition applies
conflicts: a ban list this large risks becoming exactly the kind of 'rules/template' the model executes mechanically rather than reasons through — the file mitigates this by always attaching a reasoned override, which is the right shape, but the sheer volume (70+ named bans) still trends toward checklist compliance over judgment in a token-constrained context window
testMethod: Section 9.G's em-dash ban is the only one with a stated mechanical test (‘if your output contains a single — or – anywhere visible, the output fails’, line 697-699) — a grep is sufficient and should be a real CI gate, not a self-report
sitesmithForm: Keep the ban+override shape (it is the correct pattern), but split it in two: (1) a short list of *absolute, mechanically-testable* bans (em-dash, specific banned hex families, wrapped CTA text) that a real script checks post-generation, and (2) a much shorter list of *judgment* bans (serif discipline, premium palette) stated as principles with one example each, not an enumerated blocklist the model must recite.

problemSolved: The single most-violated stylistic LLM tell (per the file's own changelog, CHANGELOG.md:36) kept recurring under a softer 'use sparingly' phrasing.
mechanism: Zero em-dashes anywhere, no exceptions, no override clause, phrased as binary ('if your output contains a single — or – anywhere visible to the user, the output fails the Pre-Flight Check').
whyItWorks: Because it is the one rule in the whole file phrased as fully binary and mechanically testable (a single regex scan of rendered text), it is also the one rule that can be verified by a script instead of trusted to a self-report.
outputImpact: Removes one specific, easily-fatigued tell; does not touch creative direction at all.
failureModes: none as written — this is the cleanest mechanism in the repo precisely because it has no judgment call embedded in it
testMethod: regex over rendered output for em-dash/en-dash-as-separator; trivially automatable, not automated in this repo
sitesmithForm: Copy the rule verbatim (it is a style fact, not expressive content) and, unlike the source, actually wire it into SiteSmith's verify.mjs as a real automated check rather than leaving it to self-report.

problemSolved: Redesigns get treated identically to greenfield builds, silently destroying SEO, brand recognition, or working IA.
mechanism: First action is mode classification (Greenfield / Preserve / Overhaul), ask once if ambiguous. Preserve and Overhaul modes require a documented audit (brand tokens, IA, content blocks, patterns to keep/retire, current dial reading, SEO baseline) BEFORE any change is proposed, followed by a fixed 'never change silently' list (URL slugs, nav labels, form field names, brand wordmark, legal copy).
whyItWorks: This is a process/ordering mechanism, not a style mechanism — it prevents a class of destructive mistake (breaking analytics, SEO, or brand recognition) by forcing observation before action, independent of what aesthetic is chosen.
requiredContext: access to the existing site/codebase to audit
contextCost: medium — the audit itself (§11.B) is a real piece of work, not a token-cheap check
outputImpact: Directly matches SiteSmith's own stated pipeline order (Truth → Proof → UX → Beta, per this repo's CLAUDE.md) and its documented rule to audit before redesigning.
failureModes: the audit is a written artifact the model produces about itself; nothing forces a second pass to check the audit was actually acted on
testMethod: none automated; could be tested by diffing the 'never change silently' list against the actual diff
sitesmithForm: Port the three-mode classification and the audit-before-fix ordering directly; port the 'never change silently' list as a literal pre-merge diff check where feasible (URL slugs, form field names are greppable).

problemSolved: Prevents shipping with obviously-known defects (unreadable button contrast, wrapped CTA text, duplicate CTA intent, mixed corner radii) that the rules above already named.
mechanism: A ~70-item Yes/No checklist the same generating model runs against its own output immediately before delivering it; 'if a single checkbox cannot be honestly ticked, the page is not done.'
whyItWorks: Checklists do catch some categories of self-evident, mechanically-describable defects (e.g. 'does the CTA wrap to 2 lines') when the model actually re-reads its own output against them.
requiredContext: the fully generated output to check against
contextCost: high — 70 checklist items re-stated in full inside the same context window that must also hold the entire design brief and generated code
outputImpact: Unverifiable in this repo whether it improves output, since there is no independent grader — see LOOPS.md and TESTING.md.
failureModes: single-pass, same-model self-grading is the weakest form of verification: a model that produced a flaw is not reliably the model that will notice the same flaw seconds later
no external critic, no adversarial second pass, no defined stop condition beyond 'all boxes honestly ticked' — 'honestly' is doing unenforceable work here

mechanical count-based items (eyebrow count ≤ ceil(sectionCount/3), ≥4 layout families across 8 sections) are the strongest items in the list because they are literally countable; the aesthetic-judgment items (serif discipline, copy self-audit) are the weakest because self-grading judgment calls is exactly where models rubber-stamp their own work
testMethod: self-report only, no external verification anywhere in this repo
sitesmithForm: Split the checklist: keep the mechanically-countable items (eyebrow density, layout-family diversity, bento cell count, em-dash scan, CTA wrap) as real automated checks in verify.mjs. Keep the judgment items as a short self-review prompt, but do not pretend a 70-item self-administered list is verification — pair it with an actual second-pass reviewer (see verification-loop skill already in this environment) for anything that matters.

problemSolved: Scroll-pin/scroll-hijack GSAP patterns are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong (trigger fires mid-scroll instead of pinning at viewport top, half a slide visible before pin engages).
mechanism: Two complete, working, copy-pasteable React components (StickyStack, HorizontalPan) with the exact ScrollTrigger config values called out as 'critical points' (`start: "top top"`, `pin: true`, `end: "+=${distance}"`, `scrub`), plus a lighter Motion-only `whileInView` alternative for simple reveals that explicitly says 'save GSAP for actual pin/scrub work.'
whyItWorks: This is real, specific engineering knowledge (a common, well-known GSAP failure mode and its exact fix) delivered as working code rather than a description — the kind of context that is cheap to load conditionally and directly prevents a concrete bug class.
requiredContext: only loaded when a sticky-stack or horizontal-pan pattern is actually chosen — conditional, not always-on
contextCost: low when loaded conditionally (as the file structures it); each skeleton is ~30-40 lines
outputImpact: Directly prevents a specific, reproducible implementation bug; does not touch creative direction.
failureModes: tied to GSAP + Motion specifically; if SiteSmith's stack differs the skeleton needs re-authoring, not copying
testMethod: none in-repo; would be caught by visually inspecting whether pin engages at the correct scroll offset
sitesmithForm: Re-express the two skeletons in our own words/code for whatever animation stack SiteSmith standardizes on; keep the 'critical points' callout pattern (name the exact config values that must be correct) since that is the actually load-bearing content, not the library choice.

problemSolved: Models claim a hand-rolled CSS effect is an official platform technology (most concretely: calling glassmorphism CSS 'Apple Liquid Glass').
mechanism: Explicit 'Honesty rule': when a brief matches a real design system, install and use the official package, never recreate 90% of it by hand; when an aesthetic has no official source (Apple Liquid Glass named specifically), label any implementation as an approximation in code comments and never claim official-package status.
whyItWorks: This is a factual/labeling discipline, not a creative one — it costs nothing to the design read and prevents a specific class of user-facing misrepresentation (claiming Apple-endorsed technology that doesn't exist for the web).
requiredContext: Appendix C skeleton only if Liquid Glass specifically is requested
outputImpact: Prevents a narrow but concrete factual-accuracy failure; no effect on visual quality.
failureModes: none identified — this is a low-risk, easy mechanism
sitesmithForm: State the general principle once ('label approximations as approximations, especially for platform-specific materials like Apple's') rather than copying the specific CSS skeleton verbatim.

problemSolved: Gives a user who has already chosen a visual direction ('I want this to look like Notion') a ready-made, fully-specified rule set instead of an open brief.
mechanism: Each is a complete, hardcoded design system baked directly into the prompt: minimalist-skill fixes exact hex codes (`#FFFFFF`/`#F7F6F3`/`#EAEAEA`, four named pastel accent pairs), exact border/radius values, an exact font-stack priority list; soft-skill fixes a numbered 'Double-Bezel' component construction method, exact cubic-bezier values, and an 8-point pre-output checklist; brutalist-skill fixes two named archetypes with exact hex palettes and mandates 'pick ONE per project, never mix'; gpt-tasteskill adds a numbered 'Bento 2.0' architecture with a literal background hex (`#f9fafb`) and 5 named card archetypes.
whyItWorks: For a single one-off build where the user explicitly wants exactly this look, a fully-specified template produces a coherent, polished result quickly — that is a real value.
requiredContext: none beyond 'the user wants this aesthetic family'
contextCost: low per-file (85-98 lines each) but each is a closed system with no design-read step at all
outputImpact: Every project built with the same fixed-template skill converges on the same hex codes, the same corner radii, the same named component patterns — by construction, not by accident.
failureModes: this IS the C-no-house-style failure mode in its purest form: three independently-briefed 'minimalist' sites built with minimalist-skill would necessarily share the same #EAEAEA borders, the same four pastel accents, the same font-stack, because the skill has no per-brief variation mechanism at all — it is a template, not a design read
gpt-tasteskill hardcodes a literal hex background (`#f9fafb`) as mandatory ('Palette: Background in #f9fafb') — there is no override path at all, unlike the flagship skill's ban+override pattern
conflicts: directly conflicts with C-no-house-style: these are exactly the kind of fixed-look generator the brief warns against, even though each individual output can look good
sitesmithForm: Do not port these as skills or presets. If SiteSmith wants named aesthetic vocabulary ("Notion-like", "brutalist"), fold the *descriptive* vocabulary (what a brutalist aesthetic connotes) into the reference-vocabulary section of the unified skill, and let the model's own design-read reasoning pick specific colors/type/spacing fresh each time — never a fixed hex-coded template.

problemSolved: Attempts to break the well-known failure where an LLM always defaults to its first/most-likely layout option across repeated calls.
mechanism: Instructs the model to 'simulate a Python script execution' inside a `<design_plan>` block: derive a seed from the character count of the user prompt modulo some arithmetic, narrate a mock 3-line Python RNG output, and use that fabricated result to 'deterministically select' a hero layout, font stack, 3 component architectures, and 2 GSAP paradigms from fixed enumerated lists.
whyItWorks: It does not work as claimed. The model has no code execution step here (no sandbox is invoked) — it is asked to hallucinate a plausible-looking Python output and then treat its own fabrication as if it were real entropy. This does not decorrelate outputs across separate calls (nothing seeds it consistently across conversations) and it does not make the model reason about the brief at all; it makes the model perform a theater of objectivity around a choice from a small fixed menu.
requiredContext: none beyond the four enumerated menus
contextCost: low tokens, but zero actual signal
outputImpact: Bounds variety to whatever is in the four small enumerated lists (1 hero architecture from a set, 1 font from a 4-item list, 3 from Section 6's small component arsenal, 2 GSAP paradigms) — the illusion of randomization does not expand the design space beyond what a plain multiple-choice menu would.
failureModes: this is the textbook example of moving a creative decision into a (fake) script rather than making the model think — the exact failure mode the C-no-mechanical-creativity brief measured at 40 vs. 59
a fabricated RNG narration adds token cost and a false sense of rigor without any corresponding gain in output quality or diversity
the menus themselves are small (4 hero options, 4 fonts) so even genuine randomization would converge quickly across many runs
conflicts: directly conflicts with C-no-mechanical-creativity: this is a rules/template generator wearing a randomization costume
testMethod: none — and none is possible, since the 'Python execution' never actually runs
sitesmithForm: Do not port. If SiteSmith wants to reduce cross-run sameness, rely on the design-read step actually citing brief-specific evidence (brand words, references, audience) so each build's direction is causally tied to that specific brief — real variance comes from real inputs, not fabricated dice rolls.

problemSolved: Same repetitive-output problem as gpt-fake-rng, applied to the image-generation-first workflow.
mechanism: "Choose 1" from each of 5 enumerated category lists (theme paradigm, background character, typography character, hero architecture, section system — 4-6 options each) plus "choose exactly 4" from an 11-item component list and "choose exactly 2" from a 6-item motion list, then commit to that combination consistently across all generated images.
whyItWorks: Unlike gpt-fake-rng, this does not pretend to be objective/randomized — it is presented plainly as 'internally choose a strong combination and commit to it,' which is honest about being a menu, not a dice roll. It does genuinely help *internal consistency* within one multi-image build (all sections share one committed direction).
contextCost: medium — the six menus plus the consistency instruction is ~75 lines
outputImpact: Improves within-project coherence (all sections of one site agree on a direction) but still bounds cross-project variety to the combinatorial space of ~4x4x6x6x6 fixed options, before considering the component/motion sub-picks — large in principle, but still a fixed finite menu rather than a design read grounded in the specific brief.
failureModes: like the dial lookup tables, this substitutes a brief-agnostic menu selection for reasoning grounded in the actual brief — two unrelated briefs that both read as 'premium tech startup' will draw from the identical 6 menus
no mechanism ties the choice back to *why* this brief specifically calls for e.g. 'Deep Dark Mode' over 'Quiet Premium Neutral'
conflicts: partially conflicts with C-no-mechanical-creativity: better than a fake RNG because it's honest about being a menu, but still a rules/template selection rather than evidence-grounded reasoning
sitesmithForm: Do not port the fixed menus. The one part worth keeping is the *instruction*, not the menu: 'pick a coherent direction and commit to it across every section' is a valid consistency rule and can be stated in one sentence without an enumerated picklist underneath it.

problemSolved: Coded output visually 'drifts' from a good generated reference image — the model generates a strong-looking comp, then implements a generic, simplified version of it in code.
mechanism: Mandatory ordering (generate reference image → deeply analyze it for text/type/spacing/color/components → implement to match), a hard rule against cropping a section out of a larger composite image (regenerate a fresh section-specific image instead, since cropping distorts spacing/proportions), and an explicit 'Anti-Drift' rule listing concrete drift symptoms (simplifying into default templates, compressing generous spacing, replacing distinctive typography with plain hierarchy) to check the implementation against after the fact.
whyItWorks: This targets a real, specific, named failure mode (design drift between reference and implementation) with a concrete, checkable countermeasure (compare final code against the specific properties named in the reference), rather than a vague 'make it look nice.'
requiredContext: an image-generation tool must be available
the generated reference image(s) themselves must be re-inspected during implementation, not just generated and forgotten
contextCost: high — generating and re-analyzing multiple images per section is expensive in tool calls and tokens, and only applies when image generation is available at all
outputImpact: When followed, directly prevents a specific, real degradation; the mechanism is agnostic to which aesthetic is chosen.
failureModes: depends entirely on an image-generation tool being available and good enough to produce a faithful reference — no fallback content is defined for when it is not
the 'deeply analyze' step is still a self-report with no independent check that analysis actually happened before code was written
testMethod: the 'Clarity Check' (§35) is a 21-item self-administered list, same weakness as the flagship skill's pre-flight checklist
sitesmithForm: Port the ordering discipline and the named anti-drift symptom list as a lightweight principle for any SiteSmith workflow that uses image generation as a design reference; do not port the image-count-per-section escalation rules (§3-4), which are Codex-context-window-specific plumbing, not a general mechanism.

problemSolved: Models truncate long code output with placeholder comments ('// rest of code', '// implement here') or stop early with 'let me know if you want me to continue.'
mechanism: A banned-pattern list for both code (`// ...`, `// TODO`, bare `...`) and prose ('for brevity', 'and so on'), a three-step execution process (scope → build → cross-check deliverable count against request), and a defined pause/resume protocol for genuinely token-limited responses (`[PAUSED — X of Y complete. Send "continue" ...]`).
whyItWorks: This is orthogonal to design taste entirely — it is general prompt engineering against a known LLM laziness failure mode, backed (per this repo's own `research/laziness/` essay) by cited effects like the 2025 controlled truncation study, though that essay itself has no working links (see TESTING.md).
outputImpact: No effect on visual/creative quality; reduces incomplete-file delivery specifically.
failureModes: the defined pause/resume protocol assumes the calling harness will actually send back the literal word 'continue' and resume state correctly — not guaranteed in every host
sitesmithForm: Fold the banned-pattern list and the scope-lock-then-cross-check process into SiteSmith's general execution discipline (not the design-taste content specifically) if truncation has been an observed problem; skip the pause/resume protocol unless SiteSmith's harness actually supports mid-task resumption on a literal keyword.

problemSolved: Attempts to justify the output-skill's prompt-engineering claims (e.g. '+45% quality from tip framing', '+115% from combined stimuli', a 'Winter Break Hypothesis' about seasonal ChatGPT laziness) with cited research.
mechanism: A `references.md` names five studies/phenomena by short label (EmotionPrompt, LazyBench, Compounding Error Avoidance, Seasonal Behavior Analysis, '2025 Controlled Laziness Experiments') with no links, no authors beyond the project name, no DOIs, no venue, no dates beyond a bare month/year for one entry.
whyItWorks: It doesn't establish anything verifiable as written. 'EmotionPrompt' is a real, findable arXiv paper by name; the others (LazyBench, the December-2025 three-part study, the Winter Break Hypothesis) are not independently locatable from the citation given, and the specific numbers quoted (+45%, +115%, 34%→80%) are asserted without a traceable source in this repo.
requiredContext: none provided by the repo itself — a reader would have to independently locate and verify each claim
contextCost: low to load, but low-trust content
outputImpact: None directly on generated pages; it exists to lend authority to the output-skill's rules.
failureModes: asserted-not-verifiable research is exactly the kind of unproven claim that should not be re-published as if SiteSmith itself verified it

even if the underlying phenomena are real (LLM truncation under complex multi-part instructions is a widely observed practical issue), citing invented-looking study names with precise percentages manufactures false confidence
testMethod: none — no links, no way to verify from the repo alone
sitesmithForm: Do not port the citations or the specific percentage claims. If SiteSmith documents a rationale for anti-truncation rules, state it as observed practical behavior ('models are known to truncate long code output under complex instructions') without inventing or repeating unverifiable statistics.
